#!/bin/sh
# chr-launch.sh: run the OFFICIAL mikrotik/chr image (MikroTik RouterOS Cloud
# Hosted Router) as a containerlab node, image untouched.
#
# The image is MikroTik's own Docker Hub distribution (Alpine + qemu +
# /diskimage/chr-<ver>.img + /start.sh). This script is bind-mounted into the
# node and set as its entrypoint by the containerlab `mikrotik_chr` kind. It replaces
# the image's /start.sh, which is not orchestration-ready (containerlab#3116):
# it scans interfaces once before containerlab attaches the links, bridges the
# management NIC so the container IP never reaches the router, and imports no
# startup config.
#
# What it does (vrnetlab's mikrotik/routeros launch.py is the model, re-done
# with the image's own busybox + qemu: no python, no ftp client, no tc):
#   1. waits for the CLAB_INTFS data interfaces containerlab attaches (eth1..N)
#   2. management, transparent: the container's eth0 is bridged with the VM's
#      ether1 tap, and eth0's addresses and default gateways move into RouterOS
#      ether1. The router IS the node's management address: management services
#      reach it directly, nothing is port-forwarded. The image ships only
#      busybox (no tc), so this uses a bridge where vrnetlab uses tc-mirred
#   3. data: one tap per container interface, bridged pairwise (ethN <-> tapN,
#      LLDP forwarded). NIC order in the VM follows the eth index, so container
#      ethN is always RouterOS ether(N+1), even with gaps
#   4. after boot, over IPv6 link-local on the management bridge (no address is
#      added to the management network): sets the credentials and the identity,
#      configures ether1 with the management addresses and keeps their return
#      path in its own VRF (`mgmt`, below), then fetches
#      /ftpboot/config.auto.rsc (the containerlab startup-config, when present)
#      from the launcher and `/import`s it
#   5. prints the ready marker on the container log and waits on qemu
#
# Restart (docker restart, containerlab restart --node): RouterOS keys an
# ethernet interface on its MAC. A NIC that comes back with a new MAC is a NEW
# device (ether1 becomes ether3) and the DHCP client bound to ether1 never
# binds. Docker re-rolls the container's eth0 MAC whenever the netns is
# recreated, so the node id that seeds every NIC MAC and the data NIC count are
# persisted in the container on the first boot and reused: the restarted qemu
# carries the same NICs in the same order and RouterOS keeps ether1..N and
# their config. The REST bootstrap is skipped on a restart; the management
# step re-runs and re-applies the container's current addressing.
#
# Architectures: the image's own qemu (qemu-system-x86_64 on amd64,
#   qemu-system-aarch64 + edk2 on arm64), KVM when /dev/kvm exists, else TCG.
# Args (the kind's Cmd): --hostname H [--username U --password P]
#   (unknown flags are ignored); credentials default to the USERNAME/PASSWORD env
# Env (all optional, set under the node's `env:`); MEM, CPUS and DISK are the
#   official image's own variables:
#   MEM (qemu -m value, default 256 MiB + 8 MiB per data NIC and vCPU), CPUS (default 1),
#   DISK (default 128M), CHR_INTF_WAIT (s, 60), CHR_BOOT_WAIT (s, 300)
# Serial console: port 5000 inside the container
#   (docker exec -it <node> nc 127.0.0.1 5000); the container itself has no
#   address on the management network.
# Ready: /.chr-launch-ready exists once RouterOS is ready (the kind's default
#   healthcheck); it is removed at every start.
# Log lines (docker logs clab-<lab>-<node>), all prefixed "chr-launch:":
#   "RouterOS ready"                   login + startup config done
#   "startup config import FAILED: …"  the router rejected the .rsc (RouterOS's
#                                      own reason, with the line number)
#   "credential bootstrap FAILED: …"   the user/password step failed
#   "management setup FAILED: …"       the ether1 address / mgmt VRF step failed
#   "data NIC check FAILED: …"         RouterOS lacks an interface for a data NIC
#                                      even after re-plugging it
#
# Copyright 2026 NetPilot Labs
# Licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

set -u

# Credentials come from the USERNAME/PASSWORD env the kind sets (no quoting
# limits on the password); --username/--password still override them.
USERNAME="${USERNAME:-admin}"
PASSWORD="${PASSWORD-admin}"
HOSTNAME_ARG=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --username) USERNAME="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --password) PASSWORD="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --hostname) HOSTNAME_ARG="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --connection-mode) shift 2 ;;
        --trace) shift ;;
        *) shift ;;
    esac
done
[ -n "$HOSTNAME_ARG" ] || HOSTNAME_ARG="$(hostname)"

CPUS="${CPUS:-1}"
DISK="${DISK:-128M}"
INTF_WAIT="${CHR_INTF_WAIT:-60}"
BOOT_WAIT="${CHR_BOOT_WAIT:-300}"
INTFS="${CLAB_INTFS:-0}"
STARTUP_CFG=/ftpboot/config.auto.rsc
# Per-container state in the rw layer: survives every restart, gone with the
# container (destroy, redeploy --cleanup).
DONE_MARKER=/.chr-launch-bootstrapped
READY_FILE=/.chr-launch-ready
ID_FILE=/.chr-launch-node-id
NICS_FILE=/.chr-launch-nics
MGMT_TABLE=mgmt
# every management object the launcher creates carries this comment, so each
# boot can find and re-apply them, and SaveConfig can leave them out
MGMT_COMMENT=clab-mgmt
MGMT_BR=br0
# eth0's addressing as last seen: a launcher re-run in the same network
# namespace finds eth0 already bridged and bare
MGMT_FILE=/.chr-launch-mgmt
SYSNET=/sys/class/net

log() { echo "chr-launch: $*"; }
rm -f "$READY_FILE"

FETCH_PORT=8080
# QEMU's QMP monitor, inside the container only: re-plugs NICs RouterOS rejected at boot
QMP_PORT=5001

# ---- disk -----------------------------------------------------------------
IMG=""
for f in /diskimage/*.img; do [ -f "$f" ] && IMG="$f" && break; done
if [ -z "$IMG" ]; then
    log "no /diskimage/*.img in this image: not a RouterOS CHR image"
    exit 1
fi
# Only GROW the disk to the floor: an image already larger keeps its tail.
disk_bytes() {
    case "$1" in
        *G|*g) echo $(( ${1%[Gg]} * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;
        *M|*m) echo $(( ${1%[Mm]} * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;
        *K|*k) echo $(( ${1%[Kk]} * 1024 )) ;;
        *) echo "$1" ;;
    esac
}
want_bytes="$(disk_bytes "$DISK")"
cur_bytes="$(stat -c %s "$IMG" 2>/dev/null || wc -c < "$IMG")"
if [ "$cur_bytes" -lt "$want_bytes" ] 2>/dev/null; then
    truncate -s "$DISK" "$IMG"
fi

# ---- wait for containerlab's data interfaces ------------------------------
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # interface names are ethN, ls is safe here
count_intfs() { ls -d "$SYSNET"/eth[1-9]* 2>/dev/null | wc -l; }
waited=0
while [ "$(count_intfs)" -lt "$INTFS" ] && [ "$waited" -lt "$INTF_WAIT" ]; do
    sleep 1
    waited=$((waited + 1))
done
log "interfaces: $(count_intfs) of $INTFS expected after ${waited}s"

# ---- qemu command line ----------------------------------------------------
# The image's own qemu and firmware, as its /start.sh selects them.
case "$(uname -m)" in
    aarch64|arm64)
        QEMU="qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -pflash /usr/share/qemu/edk2-aarch64-code.fd"
        PCI_BRIDGES=0
        TCG_CPU="-cpu cortex-a57" ;;
    *)
        QEMU="qemu-system-x86_64"
        PCI_BRIDGES=1
        TCG_CPU="" ;;
esac
if [ -e /dev/kvm ]; then
    ACCEL="-cpu host -accel kvm"
else
    ACCEL="$TCG_CPU -accel tcg,split-wx=on"
    log "no /dev/kvm: running under TCG emulation (slow boot)"
fi

# MACs: unique per node AND per NIC. The container's eth0 MAC is unique per
# node, so its LAST TWO octets identify the node; the NIC's last byte is the
# interface index (00 = mgmt, 01 = ether2, …). Two nodes sharing a NIC MAC on
# a link drop each other's frames as their own. The id is read on the FIRST
# boot only and persisted (see Restart in the header).
node_id="$(cat "$ID_FILE" 2>/dev/null)"
case "$node_id" in
    [0-9a-f][0-9a-f]:[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]) ;;
    *)
        e="$(cat "$SYSNET/eth0/address" 2>/dev/null)"
        if [ -n "$e" ]; then
            o2="${e##*:}"; rest_mac="${e%:*}"; o1="${rest_mac##*:}"
            node_id="$o1:$o2"
        else
            node_id="$(hexdump -n2 -e '2/1 "%02x:"' /dev/urandom | sed 's/:$//')"
        fi
        printf '%s\n' "$node_id" > "$ID_FILE" 2>/dev/null \
            || log "node id $node_id not persisted: a restart will renumber the NICs"
        ;;
esac
NET="-netdev tap,id=mgmt,ifname=tap0,script=no,downscript=no -device virtio-net,netdev=mgmt,mac=52:54:00:$node_id:00"
nic_mac() { # nic_mac <index>: the data NIC's MAC, its index in the last octet
    printf '52:54:00:%s:%02x' "$node_id" "$1"
}

check_nic_index() { # check_nic_index <max-index>: reject indices beyond the NIC layout
    # 63 NICs behind bridges are tested. More run into the guest's interrupt
    # vectors (about 100 NICs per vCPU) and SeaBIOS's PCI I/O space (8 bridges).
    if [ "$PCI_BRIDGES" = 1 ] && [ "$1" -gt 63 ]; then
        log "at most 63 data NICs are supported (eth63 / ether64); index $1 is beyond the tested limit"
        return 1
    fi
    # Without bridges (arm64 virt) one bus holds the disk, management and 29 data NICs.
    if [ "$PCI_BRIDGES" != 1 ] && [ "$1" -gt 29 ]; then
        log "at most 29 data NICs fit without PCI bridges (eth29 / ether30); index $1 leaves no PCI slot for the disk"
        return 1
    fi
}

data_nic_device() { # data_nic_device <index> <mac>: the NIC's -device value (also used to re-plug it)
    case "$PCI_BRIDGES" in
        1)
            # The default PC has only 29 free PCI slots, including management.
            # Keep management on the root bus and put data NICs behind bridges.
            # Follow vrnetlab's conservative allocation of 25 NICs per bridge.
            # Omit PXE ROMs to avoid exhausting SeaBIOS option-ROM space.
            # Keep MSI-X, but share one vector between RX/TX queues (plus one
            # for config) to reduce IRQ pressure.
            # Disabling MSI-X entirely can leave NICs missing in RouterOS.
            printf '%s' "virtio-net,id=nic$1,netdev=d$1,mac=$2,bus=chrpci$(( ($1 - 1) / 25 + 1 )),addr=$(printf '0x%x' $(( ($1 - 1) % 25 + 1 ))),romfile=,vectors=2"
            ;;
        *)
            # ARM64 uses the virt machine and keeps its existing NIC layout.
            printf '%s' "virtio-net,id=nic$1,netdev=d$1,mac=$2"
            ;;
    esac
}

qemu_data_nic() { # qemu_data_nic <index> <mac>: append-only QEMU arguments
    # Each bridge comes right before its first NIC.
    if [ "$PCI_BRIDGES" = 1 ] && [ $(( ($1 - 1) % 25 )) -eq 0 ]; then
        _bridge=$(( ($1 - 1) / 25 + 1 ))
        printf '%s ' "-device pci-bridge,id=chrpci$_bridge,chassis_nr=$_bridge,bus=pci.0"
    fi
    printf '%s' "-netdev tap,id=d$1,ifname=tap$1,script=no,downscript=no -device $(data_nic_device "$1" "$2")"
}

# ---- management: eth0 + tap0 on one bridge, eth0's addressing to the VM ----
ip_global() { # ip_global <4|6> <dev>: the first global address/prefix
    ip -"$1" addr show dev "$2" 2>/dev/null \
        | sed -n '/scope global/s/^ *inet6\{0,1\} \([^ ]*\) .*/\1/p' | head -n1
}
ip_gw() { # ip_gw <4|6>: the default gateway
    ip -"$1" route show default 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^default via \([^ ]*\) .*/\1/p' | head -n1
}
M4="$(ip_global 4 eth0)"; M6="$(ip_global 6 eth0)"
G4="$(ip_gw 4)"; G6="$(ip_gw 6)"
if [ -n "$M4$M6" ]; then
    printf 'M4=%s\nM6=%s\nG4=%s\nG6=%s\n' "$M4" "$M6" "$G4" "$G6" > "$MGMT_FILE" 2>/dev/null || true
elif [ -f "$MGMT_FILE" ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1090  # written by this script, four plain assignments
    . "$MGMT_FILE"
fi
log "management: ${M4:-no IPv4}${M6:+, $M6} via ${G4:-no gateway}${G6:+, $G6}"

tunctl -t tap0 >/dev/null 2>&1 || ip tuntap add dev tap0 mode tap
if [ ! -e "$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR" ]; then
    _mtu="$(cat "$SYSNET/eth0/mtu" 2>/dev/null || echo 1500)"
    ip addr flush dev eth0
    # The launcher's side of the bootstrap channel: IPv6 link-local on the
    # bridge only. eth0 and tap0 are plain bridge ports.
    sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6=0 net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra=0 2>/dev/null
    brctl addbr "$MGMT_BR"
    brctl setfd "$MGMT_BR" 0 2>/dev/null
    echo 16384 > "$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR/bridge/group_fwd_mask" 2>/dev/null
    ip link set "$MGMT_BR" address "52:54:01:$node_id:00"
    ip link set tap0 mtu "$_mtu"
    ip link set "$MGMT_BR" mtu "$_mtu"
    # eth0 joins the bridge only once ether1 is configured (mgmt_attach): until
    # then nothing the router sends (its boot-time router advertisements, CHR's
    # DHCP discovers) reaches the management network.
    brctl addif "$MGMT_BR" tap0
    sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.eth0.disable_ipv6=1 net.ipv6.conf.tap0.disable_ipv6=1 \
        "net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.disable_ipv6=0" "net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.accept_ra=0" \
        "net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.router_solicitations=0" 2>/dev/null
fi
ip link set tap0 up
ip link set "$MGMT_BR" up
# RouterOS's ether1 link-local address, from the MAC this script gives it
VM_LL="fe80::5054:ff:fe${node_id%%:*}:${node_id##*:}00"
VM_EP="$VM_LL%$MGMT_BR"
# The bridge's own link-local address (the startup-config fetch source). Read
# once qemu runs: until then tap0, the bridge's only port, has no carrier and
# the address stays tentative.
LL=""
bridge_ll() {
    _w=0
    while [ -z "$LL" ] && [ "$_w" -lt 20 ]; do
        LL="$(ip -6 addr show dev "$MGMT_BR" 2>/dev/null | grep -v tentative \
            | sed -n 's/^ *inet6 \(fe80::[^/]*\)\/64 .*/\1/p' | head -n1)"
        [ -n "$LL" ] || { sleep 1; _w=$((_w + 1)); }
    done
    [ -n "$LL" ] || log "no IPv6 link-local on $MGMT_BR"
}

# NIC order = PCI order = the order of the -device args below. Walk
# eth1..ethMAX so a gap (links on ether2 and ether5 only) keeps RouterOS
# numbering aligned: a missing ethN still gets a tap, just no bridge. The count
# never shrinks across restarts: a `docker restart` recreates the netns and
# every lab veth of the node is gone, and a NIC absent for one boot loses the
# config bound to it. The tap keeps ether(N+1) a real interface, its link comes
# back when containerlab restores the veth or the lab is redeployed.
max=0
for d in "$SYSNET"/eth[1-9]*; do
    [ -e "$d" ] || continue
    n="${d##*/eth}"
    [ "$n" -gt "$max" ] && max="$n"
done
prev="$(cat "$NICS_FILE" 2>/dev/null)"
case "$prev" in *[!0-9]*|"") prev=0 ;; esac
[ "$prev" -gt "$max" ] && max="$prev"
# The wait above can end short of CLAB_INTFS on a large lab (links attach after
# every container started): the NIC set still spans the expected count, and
# the watcher bridges the late veths.
case "$INTFS" in *[!0-9]*|"") INTFS=0 ;; esac
[ "$INTFS" -gt "$max" ] && max="$INTFS"
check_nic_index "$max" || exit 1
[ "$max" -gt "$prev" ] && { printf '%s\n' "$max" > "$NICS_FILE" 2>/dev/null || true; }

# RouterOS v7 memory ≈ 256 + 8·CPUS·(ifaces) MiB (MikroTik CHR system
# requirements). Scale by the HIGHEST generated NIC, not CLAB_INTFS: a sparse
# link on ether64 means CLAB_INTFS=1 yet 63 data NICs are created below.
if [ -z "${MEM:-}" ]; then
    MEM=$((256 + 8 * CPUS * max))
fi

bridge_eth() { # bridge_eth <i>: container ethI joins brI beside tapI (brI made once)
    _mtu="$(cat "$SYSNET/eth$1/mtu" 2>/dev/null || echo 1500)"
    if [ ! -e "$SYSNET/br$1" ]; then
        brctl addbr "br$1"
        ip link set "br$1" mtu "$_mtu"
        ip link set "tap$1" mtu "$_mtu"
        # forward LLDP (01:80:c2:00:00:0e, bit 14); STP/LACP cannot cross a bridge
        echo 16384 > "$SYSNET/br$1/bridge/group_fwd_mask" 2>/dev/null
        brctl addif "br$1" "tap$1"
    fi
    brctl addif "br$1" "eth$1"
    ip link set "eth$1" up
    ip link set "br$1" up
}
# A veth that lands or returns while qemu runs (containerlab restores a link
# right after a restart --node, a large lab attaches late, a peer node's
# redeploy recreates the pair) joins its bridge as it appears, so the RouterOS
# interface behind tapN gets its link back without a restart here.
watch_links() {
    _warned=""
    while kill -0 "$QEMU_PID" 2>/dev/null; do
        i=1
        while [ "$i" -le "$max" ]; do
            if [ -e "$SYSNET/eth$i" ] && [ ! -e "$SYSNET/br$i/brif/eth$i" ]; then
                bridge_eth "$i" && log "link eth$i attached: bridged to tap$i"
            fi
            i=$((i + 1))
        done
        for d in "$SYSNET"/eth[1-9]*; do
            [ -e "$d" ] || continue
            n="${d##*/eth}"
            [ "$n" -gt "$max" ] || continue
            case " $_warned " in *" $n "*) continue ;; esac
            _warned="$_warned $n"
            log "link eth$n attached after qemu started with $max data NICs: no RouterOS interface for it until the node is restarted"
        done
        sleep 2
    done
}

i=1
while [ "$i" -le "$max" ]; do
    tap="tap$i"

# ---- REST helpers ---------------------------------------------------------
json_str() { printf '%s' "$1" | sed 's/\\/\\\\/g; s/"/\\"/g'; }
rest() { # rest <user:pass> <path> [json]
    # Basic auth in a header, never in the URL: a password containing a URI
    # delimiter (#, ?, /) would change where the authority ends. REST_T is the
    # read timeout (default 20s).
    _auth="Authorization: Basic $(printf '%s' "$1" | base64 | tr -d '\n')"
    if [ $# -ge 3 ]; then
        wget -q -O- -T "${REST_T:-20}" --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
            --header "$_auth" --post-data "$3" "http://[$VM_EP]/rest/$2" 2>/dev/null
    else
        wget -q -O- -T "${REST_T:-20}" --header "$_auth" "http://[$VM_EP]/rest/$2" 2>/dev/null
    fi
}
# busybox wget discards the body of an HTTP error response, and RouterOS puts
# its diagnosis ONLY there ({"detail":"Script Error: … (line N column M)"}; its
# /log stays silent). So the calls whose failure must be readable go over a raw
# HTTP POST through busybox nc. busybox nc exits the moment stdin hits EOF,
# reply or not, and RouterOS keeps the connection open despite
# `Connection: close`, so the request side is held open on a fifo and closed
# once Content-Length bytes of body have arrived.
resp_complete() { # resp_complete <file>: headers + Content-Length bytes of body arrived
    _cl="$(grep -i -m1 '^Content-Length:' "$1" 2>/dev/null | tr -dc '0-9')"
    [ -n "$_cl" ] || return 1
    grep -q -m1 '^\r*$' "$1" 2>/dev/null || return 1
    [ "$(sed '1,/^\r*$/d' "$1" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')" -ge "$_cl" ]
}
rest_raw() { # rest_raw <user:pass> <path> <json> <timeout-s>  -> "<status> <body>"
    _f="/tmp/chr-rest.$$"; rm -f "$_f" "$_f.out"; mkfifo "$_f" || return 1
    timeout "$(( $4 + 5 ))" nc "$VM_EP" 80 <"$_f" >"$_f.out" 2>/dev/null &
    _pid=$!
    exec 7>"$_f"
    printf 'POST /rest/%s HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: [%s]\r\nAuthorization: Basic %s\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %s\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n%s' \
        "$2" "$VM_LL" "$(printf '%s' "$1" | base64 | tr -d '\n')" \
        "$(printf '%s' "$3" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')" "$3" >&7
    _left=$4
    while kill -0 "$_pid" 2>/dev/null && ! resp_complete "$_f.out" && [ "$_left" -gt 0 ]; do
        sleep 1; _left=$(( _left - 1 ))
    done
    exec 7>&-
    wait "$_pid" 2>/dev/null
    _st="$(head -n1 "$_f.out" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | cut -d' ' -f2)"
    _body="$(sed '1,/^\r*$/d' "$_f.out" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')"
    rm -f "$_f" "$_f.out"
    printf '%s %s' "${_st:-000}" "$_body"
}
# RouterOS REST returns the object/array on success and an empty body for a
# bare `set`: only an explicit error object is a failure here. A silently
# failed call is caught by the read-back checks that follow each step.
is_err() { case "$1" in *'"error"'*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac; }

# ---- wait for RouterOS ----------------------------------------------------
waited=0
AUTH=""
# A fresh official CHR disk has ONLY the factory `admin` account (blank
# password): the first boot authenticates as that account whatever --username
# asks for, and the requested user is created below. On a restart the pair that
# answers is the requested user.
while [ -z "$AUTH" ]; do
    for _cred in "admin:" "admin:$PASSWORD" "$USERNAME:$PASSWORD"; do
        rest "$_cred" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 && { AUTH="$_cred"; break; }
    done
    [ -n "$AUTH" ] && break
    if ! kill -0 "$QEMU_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
        log "qemu exited during boot"
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 2
    waited=$((waited + 2))
    if [ "$waited" -ge "$BOOT_WAIT" ]; then
        log "RouterOS did not answer within ${BOOT_WAIT}s: leaving qemu running"
        wait "$QEMU_PID"
        exit 1
    fi
done

# ---- data NICs: every one must be a RouterOS interface ----------------------
# RouterOS's kernel can veto a virtio NIC that registers while RouterOS itself
# starts up: the driver's probe fails with -1 and the interface never appears.
# With more than about 33 NICs one or more are hit, and which one depends on
# timing. The NIC itself is fine: plugged in again after boot it registers
# normally, and RouterOS re-attaches the port's config, which it keys by MAC.
# So wait until the interface list stops growing, then re-plug every NIC
# RouterOS lacks, at the same PCI address.
ros_macs() { # the orig-mac-address of every RouterOS ethernet interface, lower case
    rest "$AUTH" interface/ethernet | tr '{' '\n' \
        | sed -n 's/.*"orig-mac-address":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | tr 'A-F' 'a-f'
}
missing_nics() { # indices of the data NICs RouterOS has no interface for
    _have="$(ros_macs)"

        case "$_have" in *"$(nic_mac "$_i")"*) ;; *) printf '%s ' "$_i" ;; esac
        _i=$((_i + 1))
    done
}
ether_names() { # ether_names <index>...: the RouterOS names of data NICs
    for _i; do printf 'ether%s ' $((_i + 1)); done
}
qmp() { # qmp <command>...: run QMP commands (one JSON object each), print the replies
    { printf '%s\n' '{"execute":"qmp_capabilities"}' "$@"; sleep 1; } \
        | timeout 5 nc 127.0.0.1 "$QMP_PORT" 2>/dev/null
}
replug_nic() { # replug_nic <index>: unplug data NIC <index>, plug it back at the same address

    # The guest ejects the device over ACPI hotplug; its id is free once it is gone.
    _w=0

        sleep 1
        _w=$((_w + 1))

    qmp "{\"execute\":\"human-monitor-command\",\"arguments\":{\"command-line\":\"device_add $(data_nic_device "$1" "$(nic_mac "$1")")\"}}" \

        printf 'HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\nContent-Length: %s\r\n\r\n' \
            "$(wc -c < "$STARTUP_CFG")"

    } | timeout 90 nc -l -s "$LL%$MGMT_BR" -p "$FETCH_PORT" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    sleep 1

        "{\"address\":\"$LL%ether1@$MGMT_TABLE\",\"port\":\"$FETCH_PORT\",\"src-path\":\"/config.auto.rsc\",\"mode\":\"http\",\"dst-path\":\"config.auto.rsc\"}")"
    case "$fetch" in
        *'"status":"finished"'*)
            # /import answers only when it finishes: a large config gets
            # CHR_BOOT_WAIT seconds.
            result="$(rest_raw "$AUTH" import '{"file-name":"config.auto.rsc"}' "$BOOT_WAIT")"
            case "$result" in
                *'"ret":"true"'*)
                    log "startup config imported"
                    ;;
                *)

                    # error: the lines before it ARE applied.
                    detail="$(printf '%s' "$result" | sed -n 's/.*"detail":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')"
                    log "startup config import FAILED: ${detail:-${result:-no response}}; lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not"
                    wait "$QEMU_PID"
                    exit 0
                    ;;
            esac
            ;;
        *)
            log "startup config import FAILED: fetch did not finish: ${fetch:-no response}"
            wait "$QEMU_PID"
            exit 0
            ;;
    esac
fi

ready

# still be inspected over the serial console, port 5000 in the container).
bootstrap_fail() {
    log "credential bootstrap FAILED: $1"
    wait "$QEMU_PID"
    exit 0
}

# ---- management: ether1 in its own VRF -------------------------------------
# The VRF owns its routing table and connected routes. Services must bind to
# it explicitly; source-policy rules are unnecessary. The link-local REST
# channel survives the handoff once www and ether1 belong to the same VRF.
mgmt_fail() {
    log "management setup FAILED: $1 (redeploy the node: containerlab deploy --reconfigure)"
    wait "$QEMU_PID"
    exit 0
}
rest_has() { # rest_has <path?query>: the GET answered a non-empty JSON array
    case "$(rest "$AUTH" "$1")" in '['*'{'*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac
}
rest_add() { # rest_add <what> <path> <json>: a 2xx with no error object, else mgmt_fail with the router's detail
    _r="$(rest_raw "$AUTH" "$2" "$3" 20)"
    case "$_r" in
        2??\ *) is_err "$_r" && mgmt_fail "$1: ${_r#* }" ;;
        *) mgmt_fail "$1: ${_r:-no response}" ;;
    esac
}
rest_count() { # rest_count <path?query>: number of objects the GET answered
    rest "$AUTH" "$1" | tr '{' '\n' | grep -c '"\.id"'
}
rest_clear() { # rest_clear <menu>: remove its clab-mgmt objects
    _ids="$(rest "$AUTH" "$1?comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" | tr '{' '\n' \
        | sed -n 's/.*"\.id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | paste -sd, -)"
    [ -z "$_ids" ] || rest_add "remove old $1" "$1/remove" "{\".id\":\"$_ids\"}"
}
# A native VRF creates its routing table asynchronously. Move the interface
# and services together in a router-local background job, then prove the
# handoff before configuring addresses/routes or attaching external eth0.
mgmt_vrf_ready() {
    rest_has "ip/vrf?name=$MGMT_TABLE&interfaces=ether1&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT&disabled=false" || return 1
    rest_has "routing/table?name=$MGMT_TABLE&dynamic=true&invalid=false" || return 1
    for _svc in ssh www www-ssl api api-ssl winbox telnet; do
        rest_has "ip/service?name=$_svc&vrf=$MGMT_TABLE&dynamic=false" || return 1
    done
    case "$(rest "$AUTH" snmp)" in
        *"\"vrf\":\"$MGMT_TABLE\""*) return 0 ;;
        *) return 1 ;;
    esac
}
mgmt_vrf() {
    if rest_has "ip/vrf?name=$MGMT_TABLE&interfaces=ether1&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT&disabled=false"; then
        # User service overrides are applied by startup-config, after the
        # first-boot defaults. Do not overwrite them on a restart.
        [ -f "$DONE_MARKER" ] && return 0
    else
        if rest_has "routing/table?name=$MGMT_TABLE"; then
            mgmt_fail "table $MGMT_TABLE already exists without the launcher's VRF; use a fresh container"
        fi
        _script=":delay 1s; /ip vrf add name=$MGMT_TABLE interfaces=ether1 place-before=0 comment=$MGMT_COMMENT; /ip service set ssh,www,www-ssl,api,api-ssl,winbox,telnet vrf=$MGMT_TABLE; /snmp set vrf=$MGMT_TABLE"
        rest_add "start management VRF handoff" execute "{\"script\":\"$(json_str "$_script")\"}"
    fi
    _start=$(date +%s)
    until mgmt_vrf_ready; do
        [ $(( $(date +%s) - _start )) -lt "$BOOT_WAIT" ] \
            || mgmt_fail "VRF handoff did not complete; inspect RouterOS script errors through the serial console"
        sleep 1
    done
    log "management VRF $MGMT_TABLE: ether1, routing table and service bindings verified"
}
# The tagged objects already match the container's addressing (a restart with
# the same IP): leave them alone, re-applying would only drop live sessions.
mgmt_in_place() {
    _want=0
    rest_has "ip/vrf?name=$MGMT_TABLE&interfaces=ether1&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT&disabled=false" || return 1
    if [ -n "$M4" ]; then
        rest_has "ip/address?interface=ether1&address=$M4&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" || return 1
        [ -z "$G4" ] || rest_has "ip/route?routing-table=$MGMT_TABLE&dst-address=0.0.0.0/0&gateway=$G4@$MGMT_TABLE" || return 1
        _want=$((_want + 1))
    fi
    if [ -n "$M6" ]; then
        rest_has "ipv6/address?interface=ether1&address=$M6&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" || return 1
        [ -z "$G6" ] || rest_has "ipv6/route?routing-table=$MGMT_TABLE&dst-address=::/0&gateway=$G6@$MGMT_TABLE" || return 1
        _want=$((_want + 1))
    fi
    [ "$(rest_count "ip/address?comment=$MGMT_COMMENT")$(rest_count "ipv6/address?comment=$MGMT_COMMENT")" \
        = "$([ -n "$M4" ] && echo 1 || echo 0)$([ -n "$M6" ] && echo 1 || echo 0)" ] || return 1
    rest_has "ipv6/nd?interface=ether1&ra-lifetime=none" || return 1
    [ "$_want" -gt 0 ]
}
mgmt_setup() {
    mgmt_vrf
    if mgmt_in_place; then
        log "management on ether1 unchanged: ${M4:-no IPv4}${M6:+, $M6}"
        return 0
    fi
    for _m in ip/route ipv6/route ip/address ipv6/address; do rest_clear "$_m"; done
    _c="\"comment\":\"$MGMT_COMMENT\""
    if [ -n "$M4" ]; then
        rest_add "ether1 address $M4" ip/address/add "{\"address\":\"$M4\",\"interface\":\"ether1\",$_c}"
        [ -z "$G4" ] || rest_add "default via $G4 in VRF $MGMT_TABLE" ip/route/add \
            "{\"dst-address\":\"0.0.0.0/0\",\"gateway\":\"$G4@$MGMT_TABLE\",\"routing-table\":\"$MGMT_TABLE\",$_c}"
    fi
    if [ -n "$M6" ]; then
        rest_add "ether1 address $M6" ipv6/address/add \
            "{\"address\":\"$M6\",\"interface\":\"ether1\",\"advertise\":\"no\",$_c}"
        [ -z "$G6" ] || rest_add "IPv6 default via $G6 in VRF $MGMT_TABLE" ipv6/route/add \
            "{\"dst-address\":\"::/0\",\"gateway\":\"$G6@$MGMT_TABLE\",\"routing-table\":\"$MGMT_TABLE\",$_c}"
    fi
    _id="$(rest "$AUTH" "ip/dhcp-client?interface=ether1" | sed -n 's/.*"\.id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -n1)"
    [ -z "$_id" ] || rest_add "disable the ether1 DHCP client" ip/dhcp-client/set \
        "{\"numbers\":\"$_id\",\"disabled\":\"yes\"}"
    # RouterOS's default ND entry (interface=all, ra-lifetime=30m) sends router
    # advertisements on ether1 too, and every host on the management network
    # with accept_ra would install the router as its IPv6 default route. An
    # ether1 entry with ra-lifetime=none keeps the RAs harmless and withdraws a
    # route a host already learned (a disabled entry does not override "all").
    # /ipv6/nd keeps no comment, so its entry is found by interface.
    _nd="$(rest "$AUTH" "ipv6/nd?interface=ether1" | sed -n 's/.*"\.id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -n1)"
    if [ -n "$_nd" ]; then
        rest_add "ether1 router advertisements off" ipv6/nd/set \
            "{\"numbers\":\"$_nd\",\"ra-lifetime\":\"none\",\"disabled\":\"no\"}"
    else
        rest_add "ether1 router advertisements off" ipv6/nd/add \
            "{\"interface\":\"ether1\",\"ra-lifetime\":\"none\"}"
    fi
    # Prove they took (a transport flake answers an empty body, which is not
    # an error by the set-contract).
    if [ -n "$M4" ]; then
        rest_has "ip/address?interface=ether1&address=$M4" || mgmt_fail "$M4 not on ether1"
    fi
    mgmt_in_place || mgmt_fail "management addressing or routes not applied"
    log "management on ether1: ${M4:-no IPv4}${M6:+, $M6}, return path in VRF $MGMT_TABLE"
}
# Keep discovery on static data interfaces, excluding management. Set this only
# on first boot, before attaching eth0: startup-config and subsequent user changes
# can select a different list, and restarts must preserve that choice.
discovery_setup() {
    rest_add "management interface list" interface/list/add \
        "{\"name\":\"clab-management\",\"comment\":\"$MGMT_COMMENT\"}"
    rest_add "management interface list member" interface/list/member/add \
        "{\"list\":\"clab-management\",\"interface\":\"ether1\",\"comment\":\"$MGMT_COMMENT\"}"
    rest_add "discovery interface list" interface/list/add \
        "{\"name\":\"clab-discovery\",\"include\":\"static\",\"exclude\":\"clab-management\",\"comment\":\"$MGMT_COMMENT\"}"
    rest_add "management discovery off" ip/neighbor/discovery-settings/set \
        '{"discover-interface-list":"clab-discovery"}'
    rest_has "interface/list?name=clab-management&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" \
        || mgmt_fail "management interface list not applied"
    rest_has "interface/list/member?list=clab-management&interface=ether1&disabled=false&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" \
        || mgmt_fail "management interface list member not applied"
    rest_has "interface/list?name=clab-discovery&include=static&exclude=clab-management&comment=$MGMT_COMMENT" \
        || mgmt_fail "discovery interface list not applied"
    case "$(rest "$AUTH" ip/neighbor/discovery-settings)" in
        *'"discover-interface-list":"clab-discovery"'*) : ;;
        *) mgmt_fail "management discovery policy not applied" ;;
    esac
    log "neighbor discovery: static interfaces except ether1 (clab-discovery)"
}
# Join the management network, then have the router reach its gateway from the
# management address: proves the return path both ways, and the ARP/ND request
# refreshes the gateway's neighbor entry when the IP was used by another MAC
# before (a redeployed lab hands out the same addresses).
mgmt_attach() {
    [ -e "$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR/brif/eth0" ] || brctl addif "$MGMT_BR" eth0
    ip link set eth0 up
    for _pair in "$G4 ${M4%/*}" "$G6 ${M6%/*}"; do
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086  # split "gateway source"; an empty half skips the pair
        set -- $_pair
        [ $# -eq 2 ] || continue
        _t0=$(date +%s)
        until case "$(rest "$AUTH" ping "{\"address\":\"$1\",\"src-address\":\"$2\",\"count\":\"2\",\"vrf\":\"$MGMT_TABLE\"}")" in
                *'"received":"'[1-9]*) true ;; *) false ;; esac; do
            if [ $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 )) -ge 30 ]; then
                log "gateway $1 does not answer from $2 after $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 ))s (continuing)"
                break
            fi
            sleep 1
        done
    done
}

# Bootstrap + startup-config import happen ONCE per container lifetime. On a
# restart the CHR disk keeps its config and the marker (in the container rw
# layer) survives, so the bootstrap (which could wait forever if the config
# disabled `www` or changed the account, or reject duplicate `add` lines) is
# skipped. A fresh deploy recreates the container and the disk, so the marker
# and the config are both gone and the bootstrap runs.
if [ -f "$DONE_MARKER" ]; then
    log "already bootstrapped (restart): skipping config"
    mgmt_setup
    mgmt_attach
    ready
    wait "$QEMU_PID"
    exit 0
fi

# ---- credentials + identity -----------------------------------------------
# Every credential-establishing call is CHECKED: the ready marker never
# advertises credentials that do not work.
FACTORY="admin:"
rest "$FACTORY" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 || FACTORY="admin:$PASSWORD"
if [ "$USERNAME" = "admin" ]; then
    if [ -n "$PASSWORD" ]; then
        out="$(rest "$FACTORY" user/set \
            "{\"numbers\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"$(json_str "$PASSWORD")\"}")"
        is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "set admin password: ${out:-no response}"
    fi
    AUTH="admin:$PASSWORD"
else
    out="$(rest "$FACTORY" user/add \
        "{\"name\":\"$(json_str "$USERNAME")\",\"password\":\"$(json_str "$PASSWORD")\",\"group\":\"full\"}")"
    is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "create user $USERNAME: ${out:-no response}"
    AUTH="$USERNAME:$PASSWORD"
    # The factory `admin` still has a BLANK password and is reachable over the
    # forwarded services: disable it so the node keeps no unauthenticated
    # full-access account.
    out="$(rest "$AUTH" user/set "{\"numbers\":\"admin\",\"disabled\":\"yes\"}")"
    is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "disable factory admin: ${out:-no response}"
    if rest "admin:" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        bootstrap_fail "factory admin still authenticates after disable"
    fi
fi
rest "$AUTH" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || bootstrap_fail "the requested credentials do not authenticate"
out="$(rest "$AUTH" system/identity/set "{\"name\":\"$(json_str "$HOSTNAME_ARG")\"}")"
is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "set identity: ${out:-no response}"
got="$(rest "$AUTH" system/identity)"
case "$got" in
    *"\"name\":\"$HOSTNAME_ARG\""*) : ;;
    *) bootstrap_fail "identity not applied: ${got:-no response}" ;;
esac

mgmt_setup
discovery_setup
mgmt_attach

# ---- startup config -------------------------------------------------------
if [ -s "$STARTUP_CFG" ]; then
    bridge_ll
    # one-shot HTTP server on the bridge's link-local address; the router
    # fetches from it through ether1 (fetch takes a zoned link-local address
    # only as `address=`, not inside a URL)
    {
        printf 'HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\nContent-Length: %s\r\n\r\n' \
            "$(wc -c < "$STARTUP_CFG")"
        cat "$STARTUP_CFG"
    } | timeout 90 nc -l -s "$LL%$MGMT_BR" -p "$FETCH_PORT" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    sleep 1
    fetch="$(rest "$AUTH" tool/fetch \
        "{\"address\":\"$LL%ether1@$MGMT_TABLE\",\"port\":\"$FETCH_PORT\",\"src-path\":\"/config.auto.rsc\",\"mode\":\"http\",\"dst-path\":\"config.auto.rsc\"}")"
    case "$fetch" in
        *'"status":"finished"'*)
            # /import answers only when it finishes: a large config gets
            # CHR_BOOT_WAIT seconds.
            result="$(rest_raw "$AUTH" import '{"file-name":"config.auto.rsc"}' "$BOOT_WAIT")"
            case "$result" in
                *'"ret":"true"'*)
                    log "startup config imported"
                    ;;
                *)
                    # RouterOS imports line by line and stops at the first
                    # error: the lines before it ARE applied.
                    detail="$(printf '%s' "$result" | sed -n 's/.*"detail":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')"
                    log "startup config import FAILED: ${detail:-${result:-no response}}; lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not"
                    wait "$QEMU_PID"
                    exit 0
                    ;;
            esac
            ;;
        *)
            log "startup config import FAILED: fetch did not finish: ${fetch:-no response}"
            wait "$QEMU_PID"
            exit 0
            ;;
    esac
fi

touch "$DONE_MARKER" 2>/dev/null || true
ready
wait "$QEMU_PID"

316: 	return strings.Join(out, "\n")
317: }
318: 
319: // continues reports whether an /export line continues on the next one: it ends in an
320: // unescaped backslash. RouterOS writes a literal backslash in a value as `\\`, so an even
321: // run of trailing backslashes ends the line.
322: func continues(line string) bool {
323: 	trailing := len(line) - len(strings.TrimRight(line, `\`))
324: 
325: 	return trailing%2 == 1
326: }
327: 
328: func launcherOwned(section, line string) bool {
329: 	if !strings.HasPrefix(line, "add ") {
330: 		return false
331: 	}
332: 
333: 	fields := strings.Fields(strings.ReplaceAll(line, `\`, " "))
334: 	has := func(kv string) bool { return slices.Contains(fields, kv) }
335: 
336: 	if has("comment=" + mgmtComment) {
337: 		return true
338: 	}
339: 
340: 	// /ipv6 nd keeps no comment: the launcher's ether1 entry is matched by interface.
341: 	switch section {
342: 	case "/ip address", "/ipv6 address", "/ip dhcp-client", "/ipv6 nd":
343: 		return has("interface=ether1")
344: 	}
345: 
346: 	return false
347: }

One design point worth checking: the test's meaningful assertions are:
1. After reboot, `/interface ethernet print count-only` returns 64 (so ether64 survived the reboot).
2. Ping across ether64 works.
3. `Node is healthy r1`.

Note the test's weakness: the reboot may not have completed within the 300s window in a way that exercises the failure path — but if the reboot never happened, ether64 would still be present (from before the reboot), so the test would pass vacuously. Is there a way to verify the reboot actually happened? E.g., checking uptime via `/system resource print` — RouterOS uptime resets after reboot. The test doesn't assert that RouterOS actually rebooted. If the SSH `Start Command` fails to reboot (e.g., command syntax issue, or the reboot is blocked), the test would pass without exercising the new watcher code. Hmm — but `/system reboot` is the standard command. Risk: `SSHLibrary.Start Command` starts a command and returns; if the command needs a confirmation prompt (RouterOS `/system reboot` asks "Reboot, yes? [yes/no]"), `Start Command` sends it in a non-interactive channel... RouterOS CLI: `/system reboot` prompts `Reboot, yes? [y/N]` in interactive mode. With SSH exec channel (non-interactive), does RouterOS still prompt? Actually RouterOS treats exec-channel commands the same; `/system reboot` would print the prompt and wait for input. If it waits for y/N, the reboot never happens, and the test passes vacuously!

Hmm, wait — let me think about RouterOS behavior. In RouterOS, `/system reboot` prints "Reboot, yes? [y/N]:" and waits. In a non-interactive SSH exec channel, the prompt would be printed and the command would hang waiting for input... Actually, from experience: running `/system reboot` via SSH exec (e.g., `ssh admin@host /system reboot`) does prompt and requires a "y". Hmm, but some RouterOS versions auto-confirm when the terminal is not interactive? Let me think...

Actually, in RouterOS, when you run a command via SSH exec channel (single command, no PTY request — SSHLibrary's `Start Command` uses `invoke_shell` or exec? SSHLibrary `Start Command`/`Execute Command` uses the exec channel by default unless `get_pty=True`). With an exec channel (no PTY), RouterOS runs the command and... I believe RouterOS still prompts for confirmation on `/system reboot`. Hmm, actually many people script reboots via SSH with `echo y | ssh admin@... "/system reboot"` — no, that doesn't work on RouterOS either because of the prompt mechanics.

Hmm. Actually, from MikroTik forum knowledge: `/system reboot` over SSH exec does present the prompt and waits. But there's also `/system reboot yes`? Hmm — RouterOS supports chaining: `/system reboot` requires confirmation. Actually I recall that in RouterOS, you can do `:execute "/system reboot"`...

The refactor is faithful: base's inline stabilization loop, re-plug loop, and failure handling become `check_data_nics()`, with the same logic and `$miss` preserved. One behavioral nuance: in base, the failure path ended with `wait "$QEMU_PID"; exit 0`; in head, `check_data_nics` returns 1 and the caller at line 538-543 does the same. Faithful.

Another subtle refactor nuance: in base, `[ "$_round" -gt 1 ] && log ...` ran only on success path (after the failure `if` exited). In head, `check_data_nics` returns 1 early if miss non-empty, so the success log only runs on success too. Faithful.

Now, let me look at one more thing I haven't fully verified: where the initial RESET vs `check_data_nics` interaction happens. The watcher starts *after* the first `check_data_nics` and `ready` (both paths). Since the event monitor only delivers events to connected clients, the boot-time RESETs (SeaBIOS/edk2) aren't seen. Good.

Now — a genuinely important check I haven't done: **does QEMU support two `-qmp` monitors?** Yes — each `-qmp` option adds a separate chardev+monitor. Well-known QEMU feature (e.g., libvirt uses multiple monitors). Confirmed OK in the prior session.

Also, is QMP_EVENT_PORT bound to 127.0.0.1 only? Yes, tcp:127.0.0.1:5002 — inside the container's netns. Not exposed to the host unless the topology publishes it. Fine.

#      busybox (no tc), so this uses a bridge where vrnetlab uses tc-mirred
#   3. data: one tap per container interface, bridged pairwise (ethN <-> tapN,
#      LLDP forwarded). NIC order in the VM follows the eth index, so container
#      ethN is always RouterOS ether(N+1), even with gaps
#   4. after boot, over IPv6 link-local on the management bridge (no address is
#      added to the management network): sets the credentials and the identity,
#      configures ether1 with the management addresses and keeps their return
#      path in its own VRF (`mgmt`, below), then fetches
#      /ftpboot/config.auto.rsc (the containerlab startup-config, when present)
#      from the launcher and `/import`s it
#   5. prints the ready marker on the container log and waits on qemu
#
# Restart (docker restart, containerlab restart --node): RouterOS keys an
# ethernet interface on its MAC. A NIC that comes back with a new MAC is a NEW
# device (ether1 becomes ether3) and the DHCP client bound to ether1 never
# binds. Docker re-rolls the container's eth0 MAC whenever the netns is
# recreated, so the node id that seeds every NIC MAC and the data NIC count are
# persisted in the container on the first boot and reused: the restarted qemu
# carries the same NICs in the same order and RouterOS keeps ether1..N and
# their config. The REST bootstrap is skipped on a restart; the management
# step re-runs and re-applies the container's current addressing.
#
# Architectures: the image's own qemu (qemu-system-x86_64 on amd64,
#   qemu-system-aarch64 + edk2 on arm64), KVM when /dev/kvm exists, else TCG.
# Args (the kind's Cmd): --hostname H [--username U --password P]
#   (unknown flags are ignored); credentials default to the USERNAME/PASSWORD env
# Env (all optional, set under the node's `env:`); MEM, CPUS and DISK are the
#   official image's own variables:
#   MEM (qemu -m value, default 256 MiB + 8 MiB per data NIC and vCPU), CPUS (default 1),
#   DISK (default 128M), CHR_INTF_WAIT (s, 60), CHR_BOOT_WAIT (s, 300)
# Serial console: port 5000 inside the container
#   (docker exec -it <node> nc 127.0.0.1 5000); the container itself has no
#   address on the management network.
# Ready: /.chr-launch-ready exists once RouterOS is ready (the kind's default
#   healthcheck); it is removed at every start.
# Log lines (docker logs clab-<lab>-<node>), all prefixed "chr-launch:":
#   "RouterOS ready"                   login + startup config done
#   "startup config import FAILED: …"  the router rejected the .rsc (RouterOS's
#                                      own reason, with the line number)
#   "credential bootstrap FAILED: …"   the user/password step failed
#   "management setup FAILED: …"       the ether1 address / mgmt VRF step failed
#   "data NIC check FAILED: …"         RouterOS lacks an interface for a data NIC
#                                      even after re-plugging it (also checked
#                                      after a reboot from inside RouterOS)
#
# Copyright 2026 NetPilot Labs
# Licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

set -u

# Credentials come from the USERNAME/PASSWORD env the kind sets (no quoting
# limits on the password); --username/--password still override them.
USERNAME="${USERNAME:-admin}"
PASSWORD="${PASSWORD-admin}"
HOSTNAME_ARG=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --username) USERNAME="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --password) PASSWORD="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --hostname) HOSTNAME_ARG="$2"; shift 2 ;;
        --connection-mode) shift 2 ;;
        --trace) shift ;;
        *) shift ;;
    esac
done
[ -n "$HOSTNAME_ARG" ] || HOSTNAME_ARG="$(hostname)"

CPUS="${CPUS:-1}"
DISK="${DISK:-128M}"
INTF_WAIT="${CHR_INTF_WAIT:-60}"
BOOT_WAIT="${CHR_BOOT_WAIT:-300}"
INTFS="${CLAB_INTFS:-0}"
STARTUP_CFG=/ftpboot/config.auto.rsc
# Per-container state in the rw layer: survives every restart, gone with the
# container (destroy, redeploy --cleanup).
DONE_MARKER=/.chr-launch-bootstrapped
READY_FILE=/.chr-launch-ready
ID_FILE=/.chr-launch-node-id
NICS_FILE=/.chr-launch-nics

ARM64 still uses a single PCI bus on the `virt` machine, shared with the disk and the management NIC; the PCI-bridge expansion applies only to AMD64.

  Line 78: * AMD64: `eth63` / `ether64`, the highest port tested. More interfaces exhaust the guest's interrupt vectors (with the default single vCPU) and, from about 200, the virtual PC firmware's PCI address space, which stops the VM before RouterOS boots.

  Line 79: * ARM64: `eth29` / `ether30`, the last data port that fits on the `virt` machine's PCI bus.

  Line 84: With more than about 30 data ports, RouterOS can reject a NIC while it boots, and the interface does not appear. The launcher checks that RouterOS has an interface for every data NIC and re-plugs the missing ones before the node reports ready; RouterOS keeps their configuration. It checks again after RouterOS reboots itself (for example with `/system reboot`), when the container keeps running. If a NIC is still missing, the launcher logs `data NIC check FAILED` and the node is not healthy.

  Line 86: Sparse interface numbering also consumes VM resources for the intervening ports; memory defaults scale with the highest index, not just the number of links.

  Line 109: chr-launch: startup config import FAILED: Script Error: bad parameter network-type (line 3 column 59); lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not

The save filter omits `add` entries tagged `clab-mgmt`, plus IPv4/IPv6 address, DHCP-client and IPv6 neighbor-discovery `add` entries for `ether1`, even without that tag. These management settings belong to the deployment and are recreated by the launcher; custom entries in those `ether1` sections are also omitted. Other interfaces and untagged configuration in other sections are preserved.

  Line 118: Saving explicitly retains an intentional `discover-interface-list=static` choice, which RouterOS normally omits as its default, so it survives redeployment. The launcher-owned discovery lists are recreated before the saved configuration is imported.

  Line 122: Repeated exports on RouterOS 7.24.5, 7.25, 7.25rc3 and 7.26beta4 can include an empty, disabled default `/system keymat-provider` entry that fails to import on a fresh router. Saving omits only that exact entry and leaves out the menu header if the section becomes empty, since RouterOS 7.23.8 does not recognize that menu. The default healthcheck's start period follows the launcher's own deadlines (`CHR_INTF_WAIT` + 4 × `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` + 90 s, 1350 s with the defaults), so a slow boot never reports `unhealthy`. A `healthcheck` set in the topology replaces the default one.

On restart, startup-config service overrides are preserved. The launcher uses HTTP/REST with the topology credentials during container startup. IMG=""
for f in /diskimage/*.img; do [ -f "$f" ] && IMG="$f" && break; done
if [ -z "$IMG" ]; then
    log "no /diskimage/*.img in this image: not a RouterOS CHR image"
    exit 1
fi
# Only GROW the disk to the floor: an image already larger keeps its tail.
disk_bytes() {
    case "$1" in
        *G|*g) echo $(( ${1%[Gg]} * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;
        *M|*m) echo $(( ${1%[Mm]} * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;
        *K|*k) echo $(( ${1%[Kk]} * 1024 )) ;;
        *) echo "$1" ;;
    esac
}
want_bytes="$(disk_bytes "$DISK")"
cur_bytes="$(stat -c %s "$IMG" 2>/dev/null || wc -c < "$IMG")"
if [ "$cur_bytes" -lt "$want_bytes" ] 2>/dev/null; then
    truncate -s "$DISK" "$IMG"
fi

# ---- wait for containerlab's data interfaces ------------------------------
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # interface names are ethN, ls is safe here
count_intfs() { ls -d "$SYSNET"/eth[1-9]* 2>/dev/null | wc -l; }

All verified. Now let me finalize the findings list. I have three P4 findings:

1. **P4 — Test can pass without the reboot actually happening** (`tests/16-mikrotik-chr/02-chr-high-ports.robot` lines 51-64). The test issues `SSHLibrary.Start Command /system reboot`, then asserts the interfaces still forward and the node is healthy. Nothing asserts that the reboot (and therefore the new watcher path) actually occurred: if the command fails or is aborted (RouterOS typically asks `Reboot, yes? [y/N]:` for confirmation, and over a non-interactive SSH exec channel the input may never arrive), all assertions pass on the pre-reboot state, and CI would certify a feature path it never exercised. Correction: assert the reboot actually happened — e.g., after the wait, check `docker logs` for the launcher's `RouterOS rebooted: checking the data NICs again` line (logged by `after_reboot` at chr-launch.sh:762), or assert RouterOS uptime reset via `/system resource print`. This is honest: I can't verify the confirmation behavior without running RouterOS, so I'll frame it as "nothing ties the pass to the reboot" + mention the confirmation uncertainty in the problem text, and coverage notes.

Actually — should this be P3? The verification-check guidance says "Recommend the smallest useful check for a concrete gap." The gap: the only CI check for the new feature can silently not exercise it. That's a real reliability concern for CI, but the test as written may well work. I'll go P4, since it's hardening of a new test, and uncertainty remains.

2. **P4 — 10-second dedup window can swallow a second genuine reboot** (`chr-launch.sh:786-788`). The comment justifies it as collapsing the double RESET of one reboot ("milliseconds apart"), but the window is 10s, so two reboots within 10s of each other result in only one post-reboot NIC check. Impact: minor; if a NIC is rejected on the second boot only, the node stays healthy with a missing data NIC until the next reboot. Suggest narrowing the window (e.g., 2s) or acknowledging with a `ponytail:` comment. Actually — is 2s safe? The two resets of one reboot are "milliseconds apart" per the comment. A second genuine reboot within 2s of the first is also unlikely... but even a 2s window could swallow a fast double reboot. The simplest correction: keep the window but note it, or make it smaller. I'll suggest narrowing to about 2s or a ponytail comment. P4.

3. **P4 — Watcher leaves the node healthy when RouterOS never answers after a reboot** (`chr-launch.sh:765-769`). `after_reboot` waits BOOT_WAIT for REST; on timeout it logs "data NICs not checked" and returns, keeping the ready marker, so the healthcheck keeps reporting `healthy` for a router that is down after a self-reboot. This matches the documented design ("The node stays ready during the reboot… it loses the ready marker only when a NIC is still missing afterwards" — lines 752-753), and is not a regression over base (base had no post-reboot monitoring at all). But since the PR's whole point is post-reboot reliability signaling, a hung RouterOS could cheaply be detected here by also removing the ready marker after the REST deadline. Correction: either `rm -f "$READY_FILE"` in the timeout branch (making the node unhealthy, consistent with the launcher's other FAILED paths) or document the choice. Hmm — careful: removing the marker when RouterOS merely takes longer than BOOT_WAIT to answer would make a slow-but-alive router unhealthy; BOOT_WAIT=300s default is generous. Also note: if RouterOS never comes back, qemu keeps running and nothing else recovers it, so unhealthy is arguably more truthful. I'll present it as P4 with that reasoning.

## Code Review: Re-check data NICs after a RouterOS self-reboot (`mikrotik_chr`)

### Summary

The PR adds a second QMP monitor (`QMP_EVENT_PORT=5002`) and a background watcher in `chr-launch.sh` that re-runs the data-NIC re-plug check after a guest-initiated reboot (`/system reboot`), while the container keeps running. The boot-time check is refactored verbatim into `check_data_nics()`, the test suite gains an end-to-end reboot case, and the docs and script header are updated consistently.

I traced the full flow: the refactor is faithful to the base logic (base lines 503–534 → head `check_data_nics` + caller), both boot paths (first boot at line 892, restart at line 804) call `watch_reboots` only after `ready` and `mgmt_attach`, and QEMU accepts multiple `-qmp` monitors with per-monitor event delivery — so the SeaBIOS/edk2 RESETs that fire before the watcher connects cause no spurious checks. The QMP event format (`"event": "RESET"`, epoch-second `timestamp.seconds`) matches the `case` pattern and the `sed` extraction. `nc` is already used elsewhere in the script, so the watcher introduces no new binary dependency, and the port stays bound to `127.0.0.1` inside the container. The CI workflow `mikrotik_chr-tests.yml` already selects `02*.robot`, so the new test runs automatically. No blocking defects found; three small hardening opportunities below.

P4 — The reboot test never asserts that the reboot (or the watcher) actually ran**Location:** [`tests/16-mikrotik-chr/02-chr-high-ports.robot` L51–L64](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/blob/5e58d57c018a01ed6ebd755f5faa4acd948a9a2d/tests/16-mikrotik-chr/02-chr-high-ports.robot#L51-L64)

**Problem:** The new test issues `SSHLibrary.Start Command /system reboot`, then asserts that ether64 still forwards traffic and that the node is healthy. Nothing in the test verifies that the reboot — and therefore the new `watch_reboots` path — actually occurred. RouterOS's `/system reboot` normally asks `Reboot, yes? [y/N]:`, and over the non-interactive SSH exec channel that `Start Command` uses, the confirmation input may never arrive, in which case the reboot is aborted and the pre-reboot state trivially satisfies every assertion. The same vacuous pass occurs if the command fails for any other reason.

**Trigger:** The reboot command fails, is aborted at the confirmation prompt, or is simply slower than expected — the test still reports green while the feature path is never exercised.

**Impact:** CI would certify the new post-reboot reliability behavior without ever exercising it, giving false confidence in exactly the scenario this PR targets. (I could not verify RouterOS's prompt behavior over an exec channel without running the lab; source-only review.)

**Correction:** Make the pass conditional on evidence that the reboot happened and was observed. The launcher already logs the line `RouterOS rebooted: checking the data NICs again` (`chr-launch.sh:762`), so the cheapest check is an assertion that `docker logs clab-${lab-name}-r1` contains it after the wait; alternatively assert that RouterOS uptime reset via `/system resource print`.

#### 2. P4 — The 10-second RESET dedup window can swallow a second genuine reboot
**Location:** [`nodes/mikrotik_chr/chr-launch.sh` L781–L791](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/blob/5e58d57c018a01ed6ebd755f5faa4acd948a9a2d/nodes/mikrotik_chr/chr-launch.sh#L781-L791)

**Problem:** `watch_reboots` deduplicates RESET events with `[ "${_ts:-0}" -gt $((_last + 10)) ]`. The comment justifies the window as collapsing the two RESETs of a single reboot, which the comment itself says are milliseconds apart — but the implemented window is 10 seconds, which also collapses two *separate* reboots issued within 10 seconds of each other. The second reboot then gets no post-reboot NIC check.

**Trigger:** An admin (or automation) re-issues `/system reboot` within 10 seconds of a previous one — for example, re-running a failed step in a lab script.

**Impact:** Low but real: if a data NIC is rejected only on the second boot, the node keeps reporting `healthy` with a missing data NIC until the next reboot, defeating the feature's purpose for that case.

**Correction:** Narrow the window to something clearly larger than the millisecond double-reset but smaller than a human re-issuing a reboot (e.g., 2 s), or keep the current value and add a `ponytail:` comment acknowledging that a reboot within 10 s of the previous one goes unchecked. Either is a one-line change.

#### 3. P4 — A RouterOS that never answers after a reboot keeps the node `healthy`
**Location:** [`nodes/mikrotik_chr/chr-launch.sh` L761–L780](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/blob/5e58d57c018a01ed6ebd755f5faa4acd948a9a2d/nodes/mikrotik_chr/chr-launch.sh#L761-L780)

**Problem:** In `after_reboot`, if REST does not answer within `$BOOT_WAIT`, the watcher logs `RouterOS did not answer within ${BOOT_WAIT}s after the reboot: data NICs not checked` and returns, leaving `READY_FILE` in place. The healthcheck therefore keeps reporting `healthy` for a router that is down after a self-reboot. This matches the documented design in the section comment ("the node stays ready during the reboot … it loses the ready marker only when a NIC is still missing afterwards") and is not a regression — the base script had no post-reboot monitoring at all — but the PR introduces the machinery that could cheaply close this gap, since the watcher is already waiting on REST.

**Trigger:** RouterOS hangs or dies during a guest-initiated reboot and never answers REST again.

**Impact:** The node is dead but reported `healthy` indefinitely, so `wait-for` stages and users relying on the default healthcheck trust a non-functioning router.

**Correction:** Either remove `READY_FILE` in the timeout branch of `after_reboot` (consistent with the launcher's other FAILED paths, which withhold the marker; `$BOOT_WAIT` defaults to 300 s, so a merely slow router is unlikely to be misreported), or leave the behavior and document the deliberate limitation in the section comment and the docs paragraph.

### Coverage notes

- Source-only review: I inspected the head and base trees of all three changed paths and their surroundings; I did not execute tests, the launcher, or RouterOS.
- Verified the `check_data_nics` refactor is behavior-preserving against base lines 503–534 (stabilization loop, re-plug rounds, `$miss` semantics, and the failure path's `wait`/`exit 0` all match).
- Verified both boot paths (first boot line 892, restart line 804) run the boot-time check before the watcher starts, and that `watch_reboots` starts after `ready`/`mgmt_attach`, so `after_reboot` has credentials and the REST channel available.
- Verified QMP assumptions from the script's own precedent: `qmp()` already drives the first monitor over busybox `nc`; QMP delivers events only to connected clients (no spurious boot-time checks); the event JSON matches the `case` pattern including the space after the colon.
- Verified CI wiring: `.github/workflows/mikrotik_chr-tests.yml` selects `01*.robot` and `02*.robot`, so the new test runs without workflow changes; `Login via SSH with username and password` exists in `tests/ssh.robot`; `TestLauncherShellSyntax` covers shell syntax of the whole embedded script.
- Docs and the launcher header log-line list were updated consistently; no stale references to "never becomes healthy" remain in the touched doc. No schema relevance: the changes are internal to the launcher script and `clab.schema.json` is untouched and unaffected.
- Unresolved uncertainty: RouterOS's `/system reboot` confirmation behavior over a non-interactive SSH exec channel (see finding 1); I could not verify it from the repository.
- The re-plug gating on `PCI_BRIDGES = 1` (arm64 never re-plugs) is pre-existing behavior preserved by the refactor, not changed by this PR.
